name: nvi
intent: Separate a class's client-facing interface from its subclass interface: clients call non-virtual entry points that own the contract (validation, locking, instrumentation, post-conditions) and delegate exactly one step to a non-public hook, so a subclass can customise behaviour but never redefine the published interface.
problem: A public virtual method serves two audiences at once - clients that call it and subclasses that replace it. Because the same function is both the published contract and the extension point, a subclass can silently drop validation, locking, logging or post-conditions, and the base class has nowhere to enforce the invariant its own API promises.
context: Base classes and frameworks whose algorithm or protocol is fixed (validate, lock, execute, notify) while one or more steps vary per subclass. Applies where the language can keep the public member non-overridable - C++ and C# default to non-virtual members, Kotlin defaults to closed members, Java and Scala use final, Swift uses non-open public members - or, in Python, Ruby and JavaScript, where the hierarchy stays under the library author's control and the hook convention is documented.
benefits: The base class owns its interface: pre-conditions, post-conditions, locking, logging and instrumentation are written once in the non-virtual entry point and cannot be bypassed by a subclass.
Two audiences get two interfaces - clients see stable entry points, subclasses see only the hooks they are meant to implement - so the public contract can evolve without breaking extensions.
Liskov substitutability is easier to keep: derived types vary behaviour but cannot weaken the inherited contract, so polymorphic callers keep their expectations.

Overload sets and default arguments stay on the public side where they belong; in C++ this removes the classic trap that default arguments on a public virtual are taken from the static type while the body comes from the dynamic type.
The invariant is tested once for the whole hierarchy: one test of the wrapper exercises the pre/post-conditions that every subclass inherits.
tradeoffs: An extra level of indirection: every operation costs a second call (wrapper to hook), and the hook is usually not inlinable, which matters for tiny hot methods.
Subclasses cannot extend the interface: they may not add overloads, change defaults or introduce new public operations, so the published surface can only grow in the base class.

In languages without non-overridable members (Python, Ruby, JavaScript) and outside the module boundary in Swift, the pattern is a discipline rather than a guarantee - a determined subclass can still shadow the entry point.
The fragile base class problem survives: a wrapper that calls another wrapper runs a hook twice, so the 'one wrapper, one hook' rule must be enforced by review, not by the compiler.
Non-public hooks hurt discoverability - API browsers do not show them, so subclass authors must read the documentation to find out what is safe to override.

It keeps inheritance as the extension mechanism, with all its coupling: base class changes are still breaking changes for subclasses, whereas a composed policy could be replaced without touching the hierarchy.

participants.responsibility: Public, non-overridable operation that defines the contract, enforces pre/post-conditions (locking, validation, logging, transaction framing) and delegates one step to a hook.
Non-public overridable method that subclasses implement or override; it is the only customisation point of the corresponding entry point and carries no invariant of its own.
Owns the algorithm and the invariant; drives the flow of control and calls its own hooks, never its own public entry points.
Provides the hooks; it does not restate or weaken the public interface.
Calls only the non-virtual entry points and is unaffected by which implementation sits behind them.

use_cases: Framework base classes that must guarantee an invariant around every subclass implementation: thread-safety (locking around the hook), transaction framing, or deterministic resource acquisition and release.
Library class hierarchies whose published API must stay behaviourally stable while implementations change, including C++ handle/body designs and the .NET Dispose()/Dispose(bool) shape.
Validation and normalisation pipelines where input must be checked and results post-processed once for all concrete readers, writers or parsers.
Testing seams: the wrapper can be exercised once for the whole family while subclasses supply doubles for the hooks, without exporting the hooks to production callers.
Cross-cutting observation added retroactively: logging, metrics, auditing or retries inserted in the entry point instead of in every subclass override.
.NET's non-sealed Dispose pattern keeps public Dispose() non-virtual, calls protected virtual Dispose(bool), and centralizes deterministic cleanup plus finalization suppression in the wrapper.

Android's View.measure(int,int) is a final framework entry point for the measure pass; custom View subclasses override protected onMeasure(...) while the framework retains control of measured-state bookkeeping.
WPF UIElement.Measure(Size) is the public layout pass while protected virtual MeasureCore(Size) supplies derived measurement logic, letting the framework own recursive layout and DesiredSize updates.
avoid_when: The varying behaviour is a policy selected at runtime rather than a subtype: pass a strategy object or a function parameter and compose it - the hierarchy buys nothing.
Only one implementation exists and no third party derives from the class: a plain non-virtual class with private helpers is simpler; introduce the split when the second implementation appears.

The language cannot express a non-overridable member and the invariant must hold against untrusted subclasses - JavaScript (and Python or Ruby without conventions) should use composition or a closed class instead.
The base class changes often or the hierarchy is already deep: composition over inheritance removes the fragile base class problem that NVI only mitigates.
The extension point would be invoked from a constructor or destructor, where virtual dispatch does not reach the not-yet-constructed or already-destroyed subtype.
anti_patterns: Making the public wrapper virtual 'so subclasses stay flexible' - the extension point and the contract are merged again and the invariant can be dropped.
Leaving the hooks public so clients call them directly and bypass the wrapper's validation, locking or accounting.
One wrapper calling other wrappers of the same class, so a single client call executes a hook two or three times (the CountingSet failure mode).
Turning every method into a wrapper plus hook pair, doubling the API surface and the class's complexity for an invariant that does not exist.
Invoking a hook from a constructor or destructor and expecting polymorphic behaviour.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: the client interface and the subclass interface are different contracts and should not share a function.
Liskov substitution: the base class enforces the contract that every derived class must honour, instead of trusting each override.
Open/closed principle: customisation stays open (the hooks) while the published contract stays closed for modification.
Information hiding: extension points are not part of the published API, so they can change without breaking callers.
Inversion of control: the base class drives the algorithm and calls the subclass, not the other way round.
Single responsibility per entry point: one operation, one hook, one step of the algorithm.
best_practices: Keep the published entry point non-overridable (non-virtual or final, non-open, final-by-default) and mark only the hooks overridable; put hooks in the least visible scope that still allows them to be implemented.
One entry point, one hook: never call another published entry point from inside a wrapper; factor shared steps into private non-virtual helpers so each hook runs exactly once.
Write the invariant in the wrapper and keep hooks free of it, so a hook cannot forget the lock, the validation or the accounting.
Document the hook contract (assumptions, obligations, allowed side effects) and use a distinct naming convention, because hooks do not appear in public API listings.
Prefer a strategy object or callback when the varying part is a policy; use NVI when the hierarchy itself is the extension model.
Never invoke a hook from a constructor or destructor, and give the base class a public virtual or protected non-virtual destructor where the language requires a rule (C++).
sources: Herb Sutter, "Virtuality" (Guru of the Week #70; C++ Report, 2001) - names the Non-Virtual Interface idiom and states the four guidelines (non-virtual interfaces, private virtuals, protected only for base calls, public+virtual or protected+non-virtual destructors).
